newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO enlargement faces growing criticism.
newsitem.headline: NATO enlargement faces growing criticism.

text.p: Smiles, back-slapping, and kisses have marked Madeleine Albright's maiden visit as U.S. secretary of state to Europe, but failed to hide growing problems over NATO's plans to enlarge eastwards, analysts say.

Albright used her debut at NATO's Brussels headquarters on Tuesday to quicken the pace of the alliance's expansion into former communist Europe by setting next December as the target date for the end of negotiations with candidate countries.

"Our goal should be to complete membership negotiations by the end of this year, so we can sign accession instruments at our meeting in December," she told North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) foreign ministers.

At the same time, America's first female secretary of state, herself a child of a divided Europe, offered Moscow new sweeteners to drop its strident opposition to the plan, including a new proposal for a joint NATO-Russia force.

"It would be a practical demonstration that we are partners rather than allies, but the real Russian objections cannot be met by military proposals. It's what we do on the political side that will count," said one Western diplomat.
On both sides of the Atlantic, the wisdom of NATO's determination to enlarge is being questioned more and more frequently.
One alliance member -- Turkey -- has also said it may block the entire project until it receives better treatment from the European Union, an issue it says is part of the wider debate.

Critics argue enlargement could destroy the existing alliance by making it unwieldy, cost the taxpayer millions of dollars, leave the countries who fail to win membership in a dangerous limbo, and alienate Russia.
"Whatever the alliance may say, it is evidently true that enlargement represents a major shift in the strategic balance against Russia," one U.S. opponent of enlargement recently told Reuters.

The Czech-born Albright attempted to deal with some of these concerns, stressing there would be a role for all states in a transformed NATO which itself would be the cornerstone of a "unified security system for the 21st century".
"The cost of prevention is always lower than that of new conflicts," she said in answer to a question over the cost of the project, estimates of which vary greatly.

Russia wants a legally-binding treaty giving it joint decision-making procedures -- a move which would essentially give it a veto over all security issues on the continent. NATO favours a looser form of cooperation.
"Russia will have a voice, but Russia will not have a veto. We will try as much as possible to work with Russia, but when we cannot, we will act as an alliance," Albright later told reporters.

The brigade idea, modelled on the ground-breaking cooperation between the former foes in the current peace mission in Bosnia, will be formally presented to Russian leaders by Albright in Moscow on Thursday.
"The Americans want to keep the pressure up -- the double message is: enlargement is on whatever you say, but look at all the goodies on offer," said one NATO official.

Albright's visits to Bonn, Paris, Brussels and London during an 11-day whirlwind tour of major world capitals have succeeded in restoring a diplomatic show of unity after Moscow had successfully exploited a number of internal differences.
A summit in Madrid in July is set to invite several of Moscow's ex-Warsaw Pact allies -- led by Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to join NATO.

If the detailed negotiations are then concluded by December, that will leave two years for the national parliaments of the alliance's 16 members to ratify the changes in time for the 50th anniversary of NATO's founding in 1999.

Several Western allies were concerned over the compressed timetable, essentially set by President Bill Clinton during his reelection campaign last summer, and worried the U.S. could be tempted to make a deal with Moscow behind their backs.

The issue burst into the open earlier this month with the surfacing of a French idea to hold a "big power" summit of Russia, the United States, France, Germany and Britain in Paris before a Clinton meeting with Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

The proposal infuriated NATO's smaller coountries, alarmed the candidate countries, and flew in the face of U.S. assurances the enlargement issue be dealt with openly and democratically taking into account the security interests of all states.
